lessons.title: Water Needs of Yam at Different Growth Stages
lessons.body:
Yam needs different amounts of water at each stage of growth. Knowing these stages helps you water correctly. The first stage is sprouting, from planting to about 4 weeks after planting. During this time, the seed yam is using its stored water to produce shoots. You only need to keep the soil moist, not soaked. If the soil is dry, give about 5 liters per plant every 3 days. Too much water now can rot the seed yam.

The second stage is vine growth, from about 4 to 12 weeks after planting. Now the plant is building leaves and vines. Water needs increase. In dry weather, give 10 liters per plant every 2 days. If you have sandy soil, which drains fast, water every day. In this stage, lack of water makes vines short and weak, reducing future tuber size.

The third stage is tuber bulking, from about 12 to 24 weeks after planting. This is when the yam tuber grows biggest. Water demand is highest now. Each plant may need 15 to 20 liters every 2 days if there is no rain. If the soil dries out now, the tuber stops growing and becomes small and misshapen. You should water deeply so water reaches the roots, which are 20 to 30 cm deep.

The fourth stage is maturation, from about 24 weeks until harvest. Now the leaves start to yellow and die back. Water needs drop. You can reduce watering to 5 liters per plant every 4 days. Too much water now can cause tuber rot. Stop watering completely about 2 weeks before harvest to let the soil dry and make harvesting easier.

A simple tool to check soil moisture is a hand trowel or a stick. Push it into the soil 10 cm deep. If it comes out dry, you need to water. If it comes out muddy, you are overwatering. In Africa, where rains can be unpredictable, always adjust based on rainfall. A rain gauge, like a simple plastic cylinder marked in millimeters, helps you know how much rain you received. If you get 10 mm of rain, that is about 10 liters per square meter, so you can skip watering that day.

lessons.title: Rainfed vs. Irrigated Yam Farming
lessons.body:
Most yam in Africa is grown under rainfed conditions. This means you depend only on rainfall. Rainfed yam works well in areas with 1000 to 1500 mm of rain spread over 6 to 8 months. But if rains come late, stop early, or have dry spells, your yield drops. A dry spell of 2 weeks during tuber bulking can cut your harvest by 30% or more. Rainfed farming is cheaper because you do not buy irrigation equipment. But it is risky with climate change causing unpredictable rains.

Irrigated yam farming means you add water when rain is not enough. You can use simple methods like watering cans, buckets, or drip lines. Irrigation gives you control. You can grow yam in drier areas with only 600 mm of rain if you irrigate. You can also grow yam in the dry season, when prices are higher. But irrigation costs money for equipment, fuel, or labour. You need a water source like a well, borehole, river, or stored rainwater.

For a small farm of 0.5 hectares (about 5000 yam plants), a simple drip irrigation system can cost between $300 and $800. That includes a tank, pipes, and drip tape. You can also use a petrol water pump to move water from a river. A pump costs about $200. But you must calculate if the extra yield pays for the system. If irrigation increases your yield from 10 tons to 15 tons per hectare, and yam sells for $200 per ton, you get an extra $1000 per hectare. That pays back the system in one or two seasons.

Many African farmers use a mix: rainfed during the rainy season and small-scale irrigation during dry spells. You can harvest rainwater from roofs into a 5000-liter tank. That water can irrigate 100 plants for a week. Mulching also helps rainfed yam by keeping soil moist longer. The best choice depends on your rainfall, your budget, and your market. If you have a reliable market for dry-season yam, irrigation is worth it. If not, invest in mulching and good soil instead.

lessons.title: Designing an Irrigation System for Yam
lessons.body:
To design an irrigation system for yam, you need to know three things: how much water your plants need, your water source, and your field layout. Yam is usually planted on mounds or ridges. For a 0.5-hectare field with 5000 plants, you need about 15 liters per plant every 2 days during peak growth. That is 75,000 liters every 2 days, or about 37,500 liters per day. That is a lot, so you need a good water source.

A simple design is a gravity-fed drip system. You place a tank on a stand at least 1.5 meters high. A 5000-liter tank can irrigate 500 plants for one day. You connect a main pipe (32 mm diameter) from the tank, then sub-main pipes (16 mm) along rows, and drip tape (16 mm) with emitters every 30 cm. Each emitter gives 2 liters per hour. If you run the system for 4 hours, each plant gets 8 liters. You can run it twice a day for 16 liters. This works well for yam.

If you have a borehole or river, you can use a petrol pump. A 1.5-inch pump can move 10,000 liters per hour. You connect it to lay-flat hose (50 mm) and then to drip lines or sprinklers. Sprinklers are cheaper but waste water and can cause leaf diseases. Drip is better for yam because it puts water at the roots and keeps leaves dry. For a small plot, you can use watering cans. One person can water 200 plants in an hour with a 15-liter can, giving each plant about 4.5 liters.

You must also filter your water. Sand, dirt, or debris can clog emitters. Use a screen filter (120 mesh) after the pump or before the drip lines. Clean it weekly. Also, plan your layout so that water reaches all plants evenly. Put the tank in the center of the field to reduce pressure loss. Use a pressure gauge to check that you have at least 1 bar (15 psi) at the drip lines. If pressure is low, water will not reach the end of the rows. Test your system by running it for 30 minutes and checking that all emitters drip. Adjust as needed.

lessons.title: Mulching to Conserve Soil Moisture
lessons.body:
Mulching is covering the soil around your yam plants with dry plant material. It is one of the cheapest ways to save water. A good mulch layer reduces evaporation from the soil by 50% or more. That means you water half as often. Mulching also stops weeds, keeps soil cool, and adds organic matter as it breaks down. For yam, which needs consistent moisture, mulching is very important.

You can use many materials for mulch. Dry grass, straw, rice husks, maize stover, banana leaves, or cocoa pods are all good. Do not use fresh grass or weeds that have seeds, because they will sprout. Also, do not use plastic sheets unless you can remove them later; they do not add organic matter. The best mulch is a mix of dry grass and crop residues. Apply a layer 5 to 10 cm thick around each plant. Keep mulch 5 cm away from the yam stem to prevent rot. You can mulch right after planting or after the first weeding.

In Africa, a common method is to mulch with dry grass from savanna areas. One hectare needs about 10 to 15 tons of dry mulch. That is a lot, but you can start with a small area. For 100 plants, you need about 200 kg of dry grass. You can collect this from around your farm. Apply mulch after rain when the soil is wet. The mulch will keep that moisture in the soil for weeks. If you use rice husks, they last longer and do not blow away. In West Africa, farmers use cocoa pod husks, which also add potassium.

Mulching has a few challenges. It can hide pests like termites or rodents. Check under the mulch regularly. In very wet areas, mulch can keep soil too wet and cause tuber rot. If your soil is heavy clay and drains poorly, use a thinner mulch layer (2-3 cm) or skip mulching during the rainy peak. Also, mulch can be a fire risk in dry savanna. Keep it away from your house. Overall, mulching is a simple, low-cost tool that every yam farmer should use, especially in areas with dry spells.

lessons.title: Drainage Management to Prevent Waterlogging
lessons.body:
Yam hates waterlogged soil. If water sits around the roots for more than 2 days, the seed yam and tubers can rot. Waterlogging also stops the tuber from growing properly, giving you small, poor-quality yams. In Africa, heavy rains can flood your field quickly. So you must plan drainage before you plant. The best time to design drainage is during land preparation.

The simplest drainage is to make ridges or mounds. Yam is usually planted on mounds 30 to 40 cm high. This raises the roots above the water table. But in flat areas, you also need drains between rows. Dig shallow channels (20 to 30 cm deep) every 4 to 6 rows. These channels carry excess water away from the field. Make sure the channels lead to a lower area or a ditch. If your field is on a slope, dig drains across the slope (contour drains) to slow water down. Do not dig drains straight down the slope, because that causes erosion.

For a 0.5-hectare field, you need a main drain at the lowest edge, about 50 cm deep and 50 cm wide. Connect all the smaller channels to this main drain. If you have clay soil, which drains slowly, make the drains deeper and closer together. You can also add organic matter like compost to clay soil to improve drainage. In sandy soil, drainage is usually good, but you still need shallow drains to stop water from pooling after heavy rain.

You can also use raised beds. Make beds 1 meter wide and 30 cm high, with 50 cm paths between them. The paths act as drains. This is common in market gardens. Another method is to plant on ridges that run up and down the slope, so water flows between the ridges. After a heavy rain, walk your field and look for standing water. Fix the drains immediately. Keep drains clear of weeds and debris. If you have a flood-prone field, consider growing yam on the highest part or making a perimeter ditch. Remember, prevention is better than cure: once tubers rot, you cannot save them.

lessons.title: Water Quality and Testing for Irrigation
lessons.body:
Not all water is safe for yam irrigation. Water can carry salt, chemicals, or diseases that harm your crop. You should test your water before using it, especially if you use water from a river, stream, or industrial area. The most important things to test are salinity (salt level), pH, and harmful bacteria.

Salinity is measured as electrical conductivity (EC) in decisiemens per meter (dS/m). Yam is sensitive to salt. If your water has EC above 1.0 dS/m, it can reduce yield. Above 2.0 dS/m, yam may die. You can buy a simple EC meter for $20 to $50. Test your water every 3 months. If EC is high, mix it with rainwater or switch to another source. In coastal areas, seawater intrusion can make well water salty. Never use seawater for irrigation.

pH tells you if water is acidic or alkaline. Yam grows best in water with pH between 5.5 and 7.0. If pH is below 5.0, the water is too acidic and can damage roots. If above 8.0, it can lock up nutrients. You can test pH with a simple test strip or a digital pH meter ($30). If pH is wrong, you can add lime (to raise pH) or vinegar (to lower pH) to a small tank, but it is better to find a better water source.

Harmful bacteria like E. coli come from human or animal waste. If you use water from a river near a village, it may contain bacteria that cause diseases in yam, like soft rot. You cannot see bacteria, so test at a local agricultural lab. If you cannot test, avoid using water that smells bad or looks dirty. Let water settle in a tank for 24 hours before use. Also, check for chemicals: if water has oil or foam, do not use it. For safe irrigation, use rainwater, clean well water, or water from a protected spring. If you must use river water, filter it through sand and let it sit in the sun for a day. Always keep your water source clean and fence it from animals.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Water Management & Irrigation for Yam Farming

Water is the single most under-managed input in African yam production â and one of the most profitable to fix. Yam (Dioscorea spp.) is a high-value tuber crop, but unlike cassava or sorghum it has a narrow moisture comfort zone. Get water right and you can lift marketable tuber yields by 30â60% while reducing rot losses that destroy entire harvests. Get it wrong and you lose not just the crop but the seed yam investment, which represents 40â60% of total production cost in most West African systems.

This practical reference distils the six lessons in this module into field-ready numbers, tables and decision rules. Treat it as your operating manual for the water component of yam farming as a business.

Water Needs at Each Growth Stage

Yam yield is built in two windows: the first 8â12 weeks after sprouting (canopy establishment) and the tuber bulking phase (roughly weeks 16â28). Stress in either window permanently reduces tuber size and grade. Waterlogging at any stage causes rot.

Table 1: Indicative daily water requirement of yam by growth stage
Growth stage Weeks after planting Daily water use (mm/day) Criticality of stress Business impact
Sprouting / emergence0â62â3ModerateUneven stands, replanting cost
Vine establishment6â123â4HighWeak canopy = low photosynthesis
Canopy full cover12â164â5HighReduced tuber initiation
Tuber bulking (peak)16â284.5â6Very highDirect loss of marketable grade
Maturity / senescence28â362â3LowMostly affects storability

Source: Adapted from FAO Irrigation & Drainage Paper 56 (Allen et al., 1998) crop coefficient ranges for root and tuber crops, and IITA yam agronomy field guidance.

Rainfed vs. Irrigated: The Business Case

Most African yam is rainfed, concentrated in the Guinea and Sudan savanna belts where a 4â5 month rainy season must carry a 8â9 month crop. The gap is where money is made or lost. A single supplementary irrigation cycle during tuber bulking can be the difference between 8 t/ha and 15 t/ha.

Table 2: Rainfed vs. irrigated yam â comparative economics (per hectare, indicative)
Parameter Rainfed (typical) Supplemental irrigation
Water sourceRainfall onlyBorehole, river, or harvested runoff
Yield range (t/ha)8â1214â20
Seed yam cost (USD/ha)1,200â1,8001,200â1,800
Irrigation investment (USD/ha/season)0250â600
Additional labour (USD/ha)080â150
Gross revenue @ USD 0.60/kg4,800â7,2008,400â12,000
Net margin upliftBaseline+40% to +70%

Source: Yield ranges synthesised from FAOSTAT (2022) West African yam yield data and IITA/IFAD smallholder yam enterprise studies; price and cost figures are indicative planning values for 2023â24 and must be replaced with local data.

Designing an Irrigation System

For yam, drip and micro-sprinkler systems outperform furrow or overhead irrigation because they deliver water to the root zone without wetting the foliage (reducing anthracnose pressure) and without saturating the tuber zone. A practical smallholder design:

  • Water source: size to deliver peak demand of 5 mm/day across the field. For 1 ha that is roughly 50 mÂ³/day â about 0.6 L/s for 24-hour pumping, or 2.3 L/s for 6 hours.
  • Emission: drip lines at 0.3â0.5 m emitter spacing, or micro-sprinklers at 2 m Ã 2 m spacing.
  • Filtration: mandatory for river or pond water â sand filter plus screen filter.
  • Power: solar pump (1â2 kW) is now cheaper than diesel over 3 seasons in most of West Africa.
  • Schedule: irrigate early morning or late afternoon; 2â3 times per week during bulking, not daily flooding.

Mulching: The Cheapest Water Investment

Mulching with crop residue (maize stover, rice straw, legume haulms) at 3â5 t/ha reduces soil evaporation by 30â50% and lowers soil temperature by 3â6Â°C. On a rainfed farm this alone can carry the crop through a 10â14 day dry spell. It also suppresses weeds â a direct labour saving of 15â25 person-days per hectare.

Drainage: Where Most Losses Actually Occur

Yam tubers rot within 48â72 hours of standing water. On flat or poorly drained soils, the priority is not irrigation but drainage. Build ridges 30â40 cm high, open field drains at 10â15 m intervals, and never plant in a depression. In flood-prone river valleys, plant on raised beds or mounds and keep a 5 m unplanted buffer along watercourses.

â  SAFETY WARNING â WATER QUALITY AND CHEMICAL RISK

Never irrigate yam with untreated wastewater, sewage effluent, or water from downstream of industrial discharge. Yam is a root tuber â contaminants accumulate directly in the edible portion. If using river or pond water, test for E. coli, faecal coliforms, salinity (EC), and heavy metals at least once per season through your national agricultural research institute or a certified lab. Do not use water with EC above 1.5 dS/m for yam. Wear gloves and boots when handling irrigation water from open sources, and wash all tubers in clean water before sale. Contaminated yam entering the food chain can cause serious illness and destroy your market reputation permanently.

Water Quality and Testing

Three parameters matter commercially: salinity (EC), sodicity (SAR), and biological contamination. Yam tolerates EC up to about 1.5 dS/m; above that, tuber size drops sharply. Test at the start of each season and after any flooding event. Many national research institutes (IITA, CSIR, NARS) offer low-cost testing â budget USD 20â50 per sample, a trivial cost against a 1-hectare crop.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Map your moisture windows: mark weeks 6â12 and 16â28 as no-stress zones on your calendar.
  2. Measure before you irrigate: use a simple tensiometer or the hand-feel method at 15 cm depth before every irrigation decision.
  3. Mulch every ridge: 3â5 t/ha of crop residue, applied immediately after sprouting.
  4. Ridge height â¥ 30 cm on all flat or clay soils; open drains at 10â15 m spacing before the rains.
  5. Size your water source to 5 mm/day peak demand and confirm with a bucket-and-stopwatch flow test.
  6. Filter all surface water before it enters drip lines â clogged emitters kill systems silently.
  7. Test water quality once per season for EC, coliforms and heavy metals; keep records for buyers and certification.
  8. Keep a water log: date, volume, source, and crop stage â this data pays for itself at loan renewal and in buyer negotiations.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO Irrigation & Drainage Paper 56 â Crop Evapotranspiration (FAO, free full text)
  • IITA Yam Research & Production Resources (International Institute of Tropical Agriculture)
  • FAO Crop Information Portal â Water Requirements
  • International Water Management Institute (IWMI) â Smallholder Irrigation Publications
  • African Development Bank â Agriculture & Irrigation Programmes

quiz.q: During which growth stage does yam need the most water?
quiz.explanation: Tuber bulking (12-24 weeks) has the highest water demand because the tuber is growing largest.

quiz.q: How much water does a yam plant need per day during tuber bulking in dry weather?
quiz.explanation: During tuber bulking, each plant may need 15-20 liters every 2 days, so about 7.5-10 liters per day.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to check soil moisture?
options: A) A hand trowel or stick
quiz.explanation: Pushing a trowel or stick 10 cm into the soil shows if it is dry or muddy.

quiz.q: When should you stop watering yam before harvest?
quiz.explanation: Stop watering about 2 weeks before harvest to let soil dry and make harvesting easier.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of rainfed yam farming?
quiz.explanation: Rainfed farming depends on rainfall, which can be late, early, or have dry spells.

quiz.q: How much rainfall is ideal for rainfed yam?
quiz.explanation: Yam grows well with 1000-1500 mm of rain spread over 6-8 months.

quiz.q: What is one advantage of irrigated yam farming?
options: B) Can grow in dry season
quiz.explanation: Irrigation allows yam production in the dry season when prices are higher.

quiz.q: What is a common simple irrigation method for small yam farms?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation is efficient and suitable for small farms, putting water at the roots.

quiz.q: How much does a simple drip irrigation system for 0.5 hectares cost approximately?
quiz.explanation: A basic drip system with tank, pipes, and drip tape costs between $300 and $800.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for a gravity-fed water tank?
quiz.explanation: A tank at least 1.5 meters high provides enough pressure for drip irrigation.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a screen filter in a drip irrigation system?
quiz.explanation: A screen filter removes sand and debris that can clog emitters.

quiz.q: What pressure is needed at the drip lines for proper operation?
quiz.explanation: At least 1 bar (15 psi) is needed for water to reach all emitters evenly.

quiz.q: How much does mulching reduce soil evaporation?
quiz.explanation: A good mulch layer can reduce evaporation by 50% or more, saving water.

quiz.q: Which material is NOT recommended for mulching yam?
quiz.explanation: Fresh weeds with seeds will sprout and compete with yam.

quiz.q: How thick should a mulch layer be around yam plants?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer of mulch conserves moisture without smothering the plant.

quiz.q: Why should mulch be kept 5 cm away from the yam stem?
quiz.explanation: Mulch touching the stem can hold moisture and cause rot.

quiz.q: In very wet areas, what is a risk of mulching?
quiz.explanation: Mulch can keep soil too wet in high-rainfall areas, leading to tuber rot.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of drainage in yam farming?
quiz.explanation: Drainage removes excess water to prevent waterlogged soil and tuber rot.

quiz.q: How deep should main drains be for a 0.5-hectare yam field?
quiz.explanation: A main drain about 50 cm deep and 50 cm wide carries excess water away.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for drainage on sloped land?
options: A) Dig drains straight down slope
quiz.explanation: Contour drains across the slope slow water and prevent erosion.

quiz.q: How can you improve drainage in clay soil?
quiz.explanation: Organic matter like compost improves soil structure and drainage in clay.

quiz.q: What should you do after a heavy rain if you see standing water?
quiz.explanation: Standing water can rot tubers, so fix drainage immediately.

quiz.q: What does EC measure in irrigation water?
quiz.explanation: Electrical conductivity (EC) measures salt level in water.

quiz.q: What is the maximum EC level for yam irrigation water?
quiz.explanation: Yam is sensitive to salt; EC above 1.0 dS/m can reduce yield.

quiz.q: What is the ideal pH range for yam irrigation water?
quiz.explanation: Yam grows best with water pH between 5.5 and 7.0.

quiz.q: Which bacteria in water can cause soft rot in yam?
quiz.explanation: E. coli from waste can cause diseases like soft rot in yam.

quiz.q: How can you make river water safer for irrigation?
options: B) Filter through sand and let sit in sun
quiz.explanation: Filtering and solar exposure reduce bacteria and debris in water.

quiz.q: What should you do if irrigation water smells bad?
quiz.explanation: Bad smell indicates contamination that can harm yam.

quiz.q: How often should you test irrigation water quality?
quiz.explanation: Testing every 3 months helps catch changes in water quality.

quiz.q: What is a safe water source for yam irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Rainwater is clean and free of salt, chemicals, and most bacteria.
